statedGuarantee: Every action an AI agent requests against a tool is intercepted synchronously BEFORE execution and does not execute unless it satisfies both static organizational policy and an evaluation against accumulated session context (intent alignment); the system supports five decisions (ALLOW, DENY, MODIFY, STEP_UP, DEFER), must not fail open, binds every action to human/service/agent/role identity, and emits a cryptographically signed, offline-verifiable tamper-evident receipt for every action. The spec is architecture-plural: conformance may be met by a protocol gateway, SDK instrumentation, or a vendor-side hook; a kernel/eBPF monitor is offered as a fourth architecture but is explicitly disqualified from standalone conformance.
advertisedRhetoric: For the eBPF architecture: "Enforcement point: Kernel level. All system calls from the agent process pass through eBPF hooks. User-space code cannot bypass kernel enforcement without kernel compromise." and "Bypass risk: Lowest of any architecture. Evasion requires kernel-level exploit or running outside the monitored environment." For the specification as a whole: "The system MUST NOT have a fail-open mode that bypasses policy evaluation" and "No effects MUST occur on target systems for denied or deferred actions." Table IV advertises bypass resistance as "High" (Gateway), "Medium" (SDK), "Very High" (eBPF), "Vendor-dependent" (Vendor).
tierSpan: An important constraint applies to kernel-level monitoring: kernel-level (eBPF/LSM) implementations alone cannot satisfy AARM conformance for context-dependent allow, deny, or defer classifications and should be positioned as defense-in-depth backstop layers alongside semantic-aware enforcement architectures.
cheapestDefeat: Worked explicitly. (1) The guarantee: no action reaches a tool unless it has passed pre-execution policy plus context-dependent intent-alignment evaluation. (2) The mechanism that must fail: the chokepoint through which tool invocations are required to pass. Because the spec itself rules out the kernel as a standalone carrier of the context-dependent half of the guarantee, the conformant carrier is always an application/network chokepoint - the MCP gateway proxy, the SDK/middleware hook, or the vendor pre-tool hook. (3) The cheapest adversary action: emit one operation that never traverses that chokepoint. Against the Gateway this is a raw HTTP request, a direct database connection, a local filesystem write, or a shell command - all four are named as uncovered in the paper's own text. Against the SDK it is any uninstrumented code path, an FFI call into native code, or a tool added after instrumentation. Neither requires forging a signature, defeating a receipt, or exploiting the kernel; a single subprocess spawn or direct socket write suffices, and the resulting child process is not itself a mediated principal. (4) The mechanism that action defeats is an application-layer chokepoint, so T3. NOTE the deployment-dependence this paper is in the corpus to test: in a layered deployment with an eBPF backstop, the narrow sub-guarantee 'forbidden actions expressed as static rules on IPs, file paths and syscalls are blocked' does survive that subprocess and is genuinely T2 - but the paper forbids calling that AARM conformance, so the document's own headline guarantee scores T3.
placementSpan: Injection: Attacker embeds malicious instructions in content the agent will process: user input, documents, emails, images, tool outputs, or persistent memory.

coverageSpans.E1: Not covered: Direct HTTP calls bypassing the protocol, raw database connections, local filesystem access, shell command execution, or tools using non-standard protocols.
coverageSpans.E2: Bypass risk: Higher than gateway architecture. Malicious code, bugs, or misconfiguration could invoke tools directly without passing through AARM.
coverageSpans.E3: Limited visibility: Encrypted network payloads (TLS) cannot be inspected without additional decryption.
coverageSpans.E4: Covered: All tools invoked through instrumented code paths, including HTTP clients, database drivers, filesystem APIs, shell execution, and custom integrations.
coverageSpans.E5: Not covered: Tools invoked through uninstrumented paths, native code called via FFI, or tools added after initial instrumentation.
coverageSpans.E6: The system SHOULD support credential scoping for minimal permissions per action.
coverageSpans.E7: Full mitigation requires distributed tracing standards and federated receipt verification that remain under active research.

schneider.surrogate: A per-action reference monitor over a syntactic predicate: pre-execution interception at a chokepoint, static policy match on (tool, operation, parameters, identity), parameter validation (type, range, pattern, allowlist/blocklist), a threshold test on an embedding-cosine semantic distance from the original request, and emission of a signed receipt. Each of these is a safety property an execution monitor can decide on a finite prefix of the action trace, and DENY/DEFER truncates the trace before the effect occurs.
schneider.objective: Non-exfiltration and intent alignment - that no composition of individually-permitted actions moves sensitive data out, and that what the agent is doing still corresponds to why the user asked. This is an information-flow hyperproperty over data that has passed through an LLM context window, not a property of any single trace, and the paper concedes it is unsolved: "Individual actions may satisfy policy while their composition violates security objectives. Tracking data flow is complicated when data passes through an LLM's context window, where it may be transformed, summarized, or paraphrased." and "Open question: Can we build reliable intent classifiers, or must we accept that some attacks will be semantically indistinguishable from legitimate operations?"

notes:
DEPLOYMENT-DEPENDENT TIER - the reason this paper is in the corpus, and the answer the rule produces. The document does NOT float between T2 and T3 by the reader's choice; it resolves itself. Section VI opens by disqualifying the kernel option from standalone conformance, and Section VI-C4 repeats it as a normative clause with a vendor prohibition: "Vendors must not claim AARM compliance based solely on kernel-level monitoring." Table IV marks eBPF "AARM-conformant alone: No*". So the T2 mechanism is present in the document but is explicitly barred from carrying the advertised guarantee; anything calling itself AARM-compliant is anchored to a T3 chokepoint. A layered deployment (SDK primary + eBPF backstop) does not raise the score, because the eBPF layer enforces only "forbidden actions (static rules on IPs, file paths, syscalls)" - it is a second, weaker guarantee running beside the first, not the same guarantee at a higher tier. Recommended corpus treatment: score T3 for the AARM guarantee, and if the SoK wants to credit the backstop, record it as a separate narrow T2 sub-guarantee rather than as a tier for this row.

EVIDENCE GRADE IS L0 AND THIS IS NOT A CRITICISM OF THE AUTHOR - the paper is a specification, self-described as such ("AARM is a specification, not an implementation"). There is no prototype, no experiment, no measured bypass, no code. Section VII supplies "Verification:" procedures for future implementers to run; none are reported as having been run. Consequently the primary adversary placement field records the placement the threat model and attack lifecycle are BUILT around (A2 - injected content in inputs, retrieved documents, tool outputs, multi-modal media, persistent memory), not one an evaluation tested, because no evaluation exists. Adjudicators comparing this row to implemented systems should weight that difference.

WHY A4 IS SECONDARY, NOT PRIMARY: the paper's central architectural claim is that the harness IS untrusted - "The AI model and orchestration layer cannot be trusted as a security boundary" and the orchestration layer "must be treated as potentially compromised". That is A4 addressed by design. It is secondary rather than primary only because nothing tests it and because the enforcement point for three of four architectures sits inside or adjacent to the same host as the orchestrator. A5 is deliberately excluded: the trust assumptions list "The underlying infrastructure (OS, network, hardware)" as TRUSTED, and "Physical or infrastructure-level attacks" are out of scope - which is honest, and is also why the eBPF option could not be scored above T2 even on its own terms.

WHY EVERY EFFECTOR IS PARTIAL. This is not a coding shortcut; it falls out of the paper's own coverage tables. Nothing reaches covered because each architecture names paths it does not reach (Gateway: raw HTTP, direct DB, local filesystem, shell; SDK: uninstrumented paths, FFI, tools added post-instrumentation; eBPF: no semantics, TLS opaque; Vendor: entirely vendor-dependent). Nothing falls to not-covered because the action model is generic over tools and the SDK explicitly claims filesystem, HTTP, DB and shell coverage when instrumented.

TWO CELLS WHERE A STRICTER CODER WOULD SAY not-covered, AND THE ADJUDICATOR SHOULD KNOW IT:
- E4 (VCS push): the words git, version control, repository, commit and push do NOT appear anywhere in the paper. I scored partial only by subsumption - a push is a shell execution or an HTTP call, both named in the SDK covered list. There is no VCS-specific span because there is no VCS-specific text.
- E5 (package install): packages, dependencies, pip and npm likewise do NOT appear anywhere in the paper. I scored partial by the same subsumption (the top-level install command is a shell execution). The DEPTH RULE independently caps this at partial regardless: third-party install hooks and the network activity they perform are never addressed, and at a T3 chokepoint a post-install hook's egress is not mediated. WARNING FOR THE ADJUDICATOR: an automated summarizer run against this paper asserted that it covers "Package/Dependency Installation: Blocking unauthorized software installation." That sentence does not exist in the paper; a full-text search returns nothing for package, dependency, pip or npm. Do not let that claim into the corpus.

E2 AND THE DEPTH RULE: the SDK covers shell execution as an instrumented call site, so the FIRST spawn can be mediated. Nothing in the paper mediates what that shell then does. There is no discussion of process trees, cgroups, seccomp, or inherited mediation for children of a spawned process at the application layer. The only mechanism in the document that follows descendants is the eBPF monitor ("Covered: All syscalls from monitored processes: network I/O, filesystem access, process creation."), and that mechanism is barred from conformance and limited to static rules. Descendants unmediated at the assigned tier means partial, per the depth rule. The same reasoning caps E3.

E6 AND THE PUBLISHED-LIST RULE: credential handling lives in R9, which is a SHOULD, not a MUST - a system can be AARM Core conformant (R1-R6) with no credential scoping at all. R9 asks for just-in-time issuance, operation-specific scoping and audit logging, but no enumeration of credential surfaces is published: environment variables, config files, OS keychains and cloud instance-metadata endpoints are never named. Undefined list means capped at partial by the depth rule, independent of the SHOULD/MUST question.

E7 IS THE AUTHOR'S OWN WORD: cross-agent propagation appears under the heading "Partially Addressed Threats" and the mitigation paragraph is literally labelled "AARM Partial Mitigation." Coding it partial agrees with the paper rather than second-guessing it. Worth flagging for the SoK honesty axis: this paper repeatedly volunteers its own gaps (partially-addressed threats, an out-of-scope list, the eBPF conformance bar, a research-directions section). Under the COVERT-CHANNEL RULE that honesty does not upgrade any cell - the side-channel section concedes that "verbose log outputs, debug traces, error messages with stack traces containing data fragments, or metadata in external API calls" bypass action-level policy, which is an acknowledged exfiltration channel outside the mediated path and therefore holds E3 at partial on its own even before the descendant argument.

UNCERTAINTY I COULD NOT RESOLVE: Architecture D (vendor integration) has no fixed tier at all - every trust property in its column of Table IV reads "Vendor-dependent", and the hooks it depends on do not yet exist in any named product. If a future SoK row wants to score AARM-as-deployed rather than AARM-as-specified, Architecture D is uncodeable until a vendor ships hooks. I scored the specification's own conformant floor, which is the gateway/SDK chokepoint.

MINOR TEXTUAL DEFECT IN THE SOURCE, recorded so a later coder does not think they found a second threat: section V-C contains a duplicated heading - "Side-Channel Data Leakage" appears twice in a row (as V-C2 and V-C3), with body text under only one of them. That subsection describes three, not four, partially-addressed threats.
